license_notes: No third-party payload file is vendored into this repository. Every statement below is written by hand for this corpus; where an entry reproduces a published technique its source names the set the technique came from.

libinjection (BSD-3-Clause, github.com/libinjection/libinjection) is the structural model for this file: raw input paired with an expected verdict in plain diffable data, the corpus itself being the reviewed artifact. No libinjection data is copied.

SecLists (MIT, github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists) and PayloadsAllTheThings (MIT, github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings) are the sources of the injection techniques relabelled here. Their files are not vendored; the payloads below are rewritten against the three engines this gate serves.
sqlmap (GPL-2.0, github.com/sqlmapproject/sqlmap) contributed ideas only, from its tamper scripts. No sqlmap code or data is present in this repository.

entries.reason: MySQL executes the contents of /*! ... */, so stmt-drop must see the DROP the comment appears to hide
the same text is an ordinary block comment outside MySQL, which is why the executable-comment rule is per engine and not universal
a versioned executable comment is live code; stripping comments before scanning is exactly the bypass stmt-delete has to survive

entries.statement: SELECT * FROM t /*!50000 UNION SELECT LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd') */
entries.reason: fn-load-file matches inside a versioned executable comment as it would anywhere else
the version digits are skipped whether or not whitespace follows them, so the leading keyword is still found by read-select
MySQL needs whitespace after -- for a comment, so this DROP is live code and stmt-drop refuses it
PostgreSQL has no whitespace requirement after --, so the same text is a comment; one universal -- rule would misjudge one of these two
T-SQL has no whitespace requirement after -- either
# introduces a line comment in MySQL only
# is an operator rather than a comment introducer in PostgreSQL, so the DROP is live and stmt-drop refuses it
T-SQL block comments nest, so the inner */ does not close the outer comment and nothing after it is code
MySQL block comments do not nest, so the first */ closes the comment and stmt-drop sees the DROP that follows
PostgreSQL block comments nest, as the SQL standard specifies and unlike C, so the inner */ does not close the outer comment and the DROP is never code

fn-dblink-exec, regression for the fail-open found in review: with block comments read as non-nesting the tokenizer ends the comment at the first */, lands on a line-comment introducer the server is still treating as comment, and everything the server does execute after the real */ is hidden from the gate; this is a single statement, so pgx's multi-statement rejection does not catch it either

fn-nextval, regression for the fail-open found in review: with block comments read as non-nesting the tokenizer ends the comment at the first */, lands on a line-comment introducer the server is still treating as comment, and everything the server does execute after the real */ is hidden from the gate

multiple-statements, regression for the fail-open found in review: with block comments read as non-nesting the tokenizer ends the comment at the first */, lands on a line-comment introducer the server is still treating as comment, and everything the server does execute after the real */ is hidden from the gate
fn-dblink-exec; the same shape with # in place of --, which is not a comment introducer in PostgreSQL at all and so cannot hide the tail even when the comment is misread

MySQL block comments genuinely do not nest, so the first */ really does close the comment and the -- that follows really is a comment; the same text is safe on one engine and a write on another, which is why nesting is a per-dialect flag
a doubled ]] is an escaped bracket inside a T-SQL delimited identifier, not the end of one
the whole bracketed run is one identifier because ]] is an escape; a tokenizer that ended the identifier at the first ] would report a second statement that the server never sees

entries.statement: SELECT N'DROP TABLE t' AS payload
entries.reason: N'...' is a national character literal in T-SQL; its contents are data and the leading keyword is still read-select

entries.statement: SELECT N'a''; DROP TABLE t' AS payload
entries.reason: a doubled quote inside N'...' is content, so the literal runs to the end and hides no statement boundary

entries.statement: SELECT N'DROP TABLE t' AS payload
entries.reason: N'...' is valid in MySQL as well

entries.statement: SELECT $$; DROP TABLE t$$ AS payload
entries.reason: a dollar-quoted string takes its contents completely literally, so neither the semicolon nor the DROP is a token

entries.statement: SELECT $tag$ ; DROP TABLE t $tag$ AS payload
entries.reason: a tagged dollar quote ends only at the identical tag, so the semicolon and the DROP inside it are data

entries.statement: SELECT $$; DROP TABLE t$$ AS payload
entries.reason: MySQL has no dollar quoting, so the semicolon really does separate two statements there
a second statement-leading keyword inside a dollar-quoted string is not a statement boundary
a dollar-quote tag cannot begin with a digit, so $1 is a positional parameter and the statement is complete

entries.statement: SELECT t.table_name, c.column_name FROM information_schema.tables AS t JOIN information_schema.columns AS c ON c.table_schema = t.table_schema AND c.table_name = t.table_name WHERE LOWER(t.table_name) LIKE ?
entries.reason: read-select over information_schema: the ? placeholder remains in the constant catalog search while its name pattern is bound separately

entries.statement: WITH pattern AS (SELECT LOWER(@p1) AS value) SELECT s.name, t.name, c.name, ty.name, c.is_nullable, CASE WHEN LOWER(t.name) LIKE pattern.value ESCAPE '!' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS table_name_matched, CASE WHEN LOWER(c.name) LIKE pattern.value ESCAPE '!' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS column_name_matched FROM sys.tables AS t JOIN sys.schemas AS s ON s.schema_id = t.schema_id JOIN sys.columns AS c ON c.object_id = t.object_id JOIN sys.types AS ty ON ty.user_type_id = c.user_type_id JOIN pattern ON 1 = 1 WHERE LOWER(t.name) LIKE pattern.value ESCAPE '!' OR LOWER(c.name) LIKE pattern.value ESCAPE '!' ORDER BY s.name, t.name, c.name
entries.reason: the statement search_schema actually sends on this engine: the @p1 placeholder stays in the constant while its name pattern is bound separately, the WITH is explained by the close of its own CTE body, and the CASE WHEN that T-SQL forces around each LIKE match reason is ordinary syntax to the gate
$1 is a parameter and not the opener of a $1$ quote, so the semicolon is a real separator and the DROP is live code
E'...' always processes backslash escapes, so the escaped quote does not end the literal and the whole tail is data
a plain PostgreSQL literal does not process backslash escapes under standard_conforming_strings, so the literal ends early and the DROP that follows is live code
MySQL treats backslash as an escape character inside '...' by default, so the same text is one literal there; a tokenizer written against one dialect finds the wrong end of the string in the other

entries.statement: SELECT 'it''s; DROP TABLE t' AS s
entries.reason: a doubled quote is content in all three engines, so the literal continues past it and hides no boundary

entries.statement: SELECT 'it''s; DROP TABLE t' AS s
entries.reason: doubled-quote escaping holds in PostgreSQL too

entries.statement: SELECT 'it''s; DROP TABLE t' AS s
entries.reason: doubled-quote escaping holds in T-SQL too
a doubled double quote is content whether the session reads "..." as an identifier or as a literal, so the two readings agree on where the token ends
fn-pg-read-file matches the unquoted content of a delimited identifier, so quoting a forbidden name does not evade it
a backquoted identifier is never a keyword, so a column named select does not read as a second statement
a U&'...' unicode escape string ends at an undoubled quote regardless of any UESCAPE clause, so its boundary is found correctly
U&"..." is a delimited identifier and its contents are never keywords
a hexadecimal literal is data; its bytes are not tokenized as keywords
multiple-statements: a semicolon followed by more tokens is a second statement
multiple-statements on the semicolon form
multiple-statements on the semicolon form, where TDS would send the whole text as one batch
multiple-statements with no punctuation at all: T-SQL makes semicolons optional, so counting them cannot decide this
the boundary rule is applied on every engine, not only on the one whose driver would forward a stacked statement
the boundary rule is applied on every engine
a newline-separated second statement carries a forbidden keyword, so stmt-drop refuses it before the boundary rule needs to
multiple-statements: a statement-leading keyword at parenthesis depth zero with no set operator before it is a new statement
a separator hidden inside a comment is not one, but the real separator after it is, and the DROP is refused by stmt-drop
